prompt:
Let $G$ be a finite group of order $|G| = 504 = 2^3\cdot 3^2\cdot 7$.

(a) If $G$ has a normal subgroup $N$ of order $8$, show that $G$ has at most $8$ Sylow $7$-subgroups, that is $|\mathrm{Syl}_7(G)| \le 8$.

(b) If $|\mathrm{Syl}_7(G)| \le 8$, prove that $G$ has an element of order $21$.

(c) If $G$ is isomorphic to a subgroup of $\mathrm{Sym}_9$, the symmetric group of degree $9$, show that $G$ cannot have a normal subgroup of order $8$.
answer: (a) $G/N$ has order $63$, so its Sylow $7$-subgroup is normal; hence $PN\trianglelefteq G$ and the Frattini argument gives $G=N\,N_G(P)$, so $|G:N_G(P)|$ divides $8$. (b) $|N_G(P)|\in\{63,504\}$ contains a group $Q$ of order $9$; $Q\to\mathrm{Aut}(P)\cong C_6$ has a kernel containing an element $x$ of order $3$, and $x$ times a generator of $P$ has order $21$. (c) $\mathrm{Sym}_9$ has no element of order $21$ (a $7$-cycle and a $3$-cycle need $10$ points).

solutions.title: Frattini argument and Sylow counting
solutions.body:
Let $P\in\mathrm{Syl}_7(G)$; $|P|=7$.

**(a)** $|G/N|=63=3^2\cdot 7$. In $G/N$ the number of Sylow $7$-subgroups divides $9$ and is $\equiv 1 \pmod 7$, so it is $1$ (the divisors are $1,3,9$). The Sylow $7$-subgroup of $G/N$ is $PN/N$, hence $PN/N\trianglelefteq G/N$ and $PN\trianglelefteq G$.

Since $P$ is a Sylow subgroup of the normal subgroup $PN$, the Frattini argument gives $G=PN\cdot N_G(P)=N\,N_G(P)$ (as $P\le N_G(P)$). Therefore
$$|\mathrm{Syl}_7(G)|=|G:N_G(P)|=\frac{|N\,N_G(P)|}{|N_G(P)|}=\frac{|N|}{|N\cap N_G(P)|},$$
which divides $|N|=8$. In particular $|\mathrm{Syl}_7(G)|\le 8$.

**(b)** $n_7=|\mathrm{Syl}_7(G)|$ divides $72$ and is $\equiv 1\pmod 7$, so $n_7\in\{1,8,36\}$; by hypothesis $n_7\in\{1,8\}$. Hence $|N_G(P)|=504/n_7\in\{504,63\}$, which is divisible by $9$. Let $Q$ be a Sylow $3$-subgroup of $N_G(P)$, so $|Q|=9$.

$Q$ acts on $P$ by conjugation, giving a homomorphism $Q\to\mathrm{Aut}(P)\cong (\mathbb Z/7)^\times\cong C_6$. Its image has order dividing $\gcd(9,6)=3$, so its kernel $C_Q(P)$ has order $3$ or $9$ and contains an element $x$ of order $3$. Let $y$ generate $P$. Then $x$ and $y$ commute and have coprime orders $3$ and $7$, so $xy$ has order $21$.

**(c)** Suppose $G\le \mathrm{Sym}_9$ (up to isomorphism) has a normal subgroup of order $8$. By (a) $|\mathrm{Syl}_7(G)|\le 8$, so by (b) $G$, hence $\mathrm{Sym}_9$, contains an element of order $21$. The order of a permutation is the lcm of its cycle lengths, so some cycle length is divisible by $7$; with only $9$ points this cycle is a $7$-cycle, and the remaining $2$ points cannot carry a cycle of length divisible by $3$. So $\mathrm{Sym}_9$ has no element of order $21$, a contradiction. ∎

prompt:
Let $R$ be a commutative integral domain with field of fractions $F$, and assume that $R$ is integrally closed.

(a) Suppose $K$ is a field containing $F$ and let $\alpha \in K$ be integral over $R$. Show that the minimal monic polynomial of $\alpha$ over $F$ is contained in $R[x]$.

(b) Let $f(x) \in R[x]$ be a monic polynomial. Show that $f(x)$ is irreducible in $R[x]$ if and only if it is irreducible in $F[x]$.
answer: (a) Every root of the minimal polynomial is an $F$-conjugate of $\alpha$, hence integral over $R$; the coefficients are symmetric functions of the roots, so they are integral over $R$ and lie in $F$, hence in $R$. (b) A factorization in $R[x]$ into non-units has monic-up-to-units factors of positive degree; conversely monic factors of $f$ in $F[x]$ have all roots integral over $R$, so by the same argument they lie in $R[x]$.

solutions.title: Conjugates of integral elements are integral
solutions.body:
Recall that the elements of a ring extension that are integral over $R$ form a subring.

**(a)** Let $m(x)\in F[x]$ be the minimal monic polynomial of $\alpha$ and let $L\supseteq K$ be a splitting field of $m$, so $m(x)=\prod_{i=1}^d (x-\alpha_i)$ in $L[x]$ with $\alpha_1=\alpha$. Let $g\in R[x]$ be monic with $g(\alpha)=0$. For each $i$, since $m$ is irreducible over $F$ there is an $F$-isomorphism $F(\alpha)\to F(\alpha_i)$ with $\alpha\mapsto \alpha_i$; applying it to $g(\alpha)=0$ (the coefficients of $g$ lie in $R\subseteq F$) gives $g(\alpha_i)=0$. So every $\alpha_i$ is integral over $R$.

The coefficients of $m$ are $\pm$ the elementary symmetric polynomials in $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_d$, hence integral over $R$. They also lie in $F$. Since $R$ is integrally closed in $F$, they lie in $R$, i.e. $m(x)\in R[x]$.

**(b)** Assume $\deg f\ge 1$.

($\Leftarrow$) Suppose $f$ is irreducible in $F[x]$ and $f=gh$ with $g,h\in R[x]$. The leading coefficients of $g,h$ multiply to $1$, so they are units of $R$. If $\deg g=0$ then $g$ is a unit of $R$, hence of $R[x]$; similarly for $h$. Otherwise both degrees are positive and $f=gh$ is a factorization in $F[x]$ into non-units, contradicting irreducibility over $F$. So $f$ is irreducible in $R[x]$.

($\Rightarrow$) Suppose $f$ is irreducible in $R[x]$ but $f=gh$ in $F[x]$ with $\deg g,\deg h\ge 1$; scaling, we may take $g,h$ monic. In a splitting field $L$ of $f$ over $F$, every root of $g$ is a root of the monic polynomial $f\in R[x]$, hence integral over $R$. As in (a), the coefficients of $g=\prod(x-\beta_j)$ are integral over $R$ and lie in $F$, so $g\in R[x]$; likewise $h\in R[x]$. Then $f=gh$ is a factorization in $R[x]$ into two monic polynomials of positive degree, which are not units — a contradiction. ∎

prompt:
Let $F$ be a field of characteristic $0$ and let $E$ be a finite Galois extension of $F$.

(a) If $0 \ne \alpha \in E$ with $E = F[\alpha]$, show that $F[\alpha^2] \ne E$ if and only if there exists an automorphism $\sigma \in \mathrm{Gal}(E/F)$ with $\alpha^\sigma = -\alpha$.

(b) Prove that there exists an element $\alpha \in E$ with $E = F[\alpha^2]$.
answer: (a) If $\alpha^\sigma=-\alpha$ then $\sigma\ne1$ fixes $\alpha^2$; conversely a nonidentity $\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(E/F[\alpha^2])$ has $(\alpha^\sigma)^2=\alpha^2$ and $\alpha^\sigma\neq\alpha$, so $\alpha^\sigma=-\alpha$. (b) With $E=F[\gamma]$, take $\alpha=\gamma+c$, $c\in F$: a bad $c$ needs $\sigma_c$ with $\gamma^{\sigma_c}=-\gamma-2c$, and distinct $c$ give distinct $\sigma_c$; $F$ is infinite and the Galois group finite.

prompt:
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over the field $F$ with $\dim_F V = n$, and let $(\ ,\ )\colon V \times V \to F$ be a symmetric bilinear form. If $X$ is a subset of $V$, write $X^\perp = \{ v \in V \mid (X, v) = 0 \}$ for the subspace of $V$ perpendicular to $X$.

(a) If $W$ is a subspace of $V$, show that $\dim_F W + \dim_F W^\perp \ge \dim_F V$. (Hint. If $w \in W$, note that $\{w\}^\perp$ has codimension $\le 1$ in $V$.)

(b) Now suppose $(\ ,\ )$ is nonsingular, so that $V^\perp = 0$. If $A = \{a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n\}$ is a basis for $V$, prove that there exists a unique dual basis $A' = \{a_1', a_2', \dots, a_n'\}$. That is, $A'$ is a basis with $(a_i, a_j') = 0$ if $i \ne j$ and $(a_i, a_i') = 1$.

(c) Again suppose $(\ ,\ )$ is nonsingular, and let $B = \{b_1, b_2, \dots, b_n\}$ be a second basis for $V$ with dual basis $B' = \{b_1', b_2', \dots, b_n'\}$. Compare the change of basis matrix from $A$ to $B$ with the change of basis matrix from $B'$ to $A'$.
answer: (a) $W^\perp$ is the kernel of $v\mapsto((w_i,v))_i\in F^k$ for a basis $w_1,\dots,w_k$ of $W$. (b) $v\mapsto(\cdot,v)$ is an isomorphism $V\to V^*$; pull back the dual basis; uniqueness since $V^\perp=0$. (c) If $b_i=\sum_j p_{ij}a_j$ and $a_j'=\sum_k q_{jk}b_k'$, then $Q=P^{T}$: the change of basis matrix from $B'$ to $A'$ is the transpose of the one from $A$ to $B$.

solutions.title: Linear functionals and the pairing
solutions.body:
**(a)** Let $w_1,\dots,w_k$ be a basis of $W$ ($k=\dim W$). By linearity, $v\in W^\perp$ iff $(w_i,v)=0$ for all $i$. So $W^\perp$ is the kernel of the linear map $\phi\colon V\to F^k$, $v\mapsto\big((w_1,v),\dots,(w_k,v)\big)$. By rank–nullity, $\dim W^\perp=n-\operatorname{rank}\phi\ge n-k$, i.e. $\dim W+\dim W^\perp\ge \dim V$. (Equivalently, $W^\perp$ is the intersection of the $k$ subspaces $\{w_i\}^\perp$, each of codimension $\le1$.)

**(b)** Define $\Phi\colon V\to V^*$ by $\Phi(v)=(\,\cdot\,,v)$. It is linear, and $\ker\Phi=V^\perp=0$; since $\dim V^*=\dim V$, $\Phi$ is an isomorphism. Let $f_1,\dots,f_n\in V^*$ be the dual basis of $A$, so $f_j(a_i)=\delta_{ij}$, and put $a_j'=\Phi^{-1}(f_j)$. Then $(a_i,a_j')=f_j(a_i)=\delta_{ij}$, and $\{a_j'\}$ is a basis because $\Phi$ is an isomorphism.

Uniqueness: if $\{a_j''\}$ also satisfies $(a_i,a_j'')=\delta_{ij}$, then $(a_i,a_j'-a_j'')=0$ for all $i$, so $a_j'-a_j''\in A^\perp=V^\perp=0$ (as $A$ spans $V$).

**(c)** Write $b_i=\sum_j p_{ij}a_j$, so $P=[p_{ij}]$ is the change of basis matrix from $A$ to $B$, and with the same convention write $a_j'=\sum_k q_{jk}b_k'$, so $Q=[q_{jk}]$ is the change of basis matrix from $B'$ to $A'$. Compute $(b_i,a_j')$ in two ways:
$$(b_i,a_j')=\sum_l p_{il}(a_l,a_j')=p_{ij},\qquad (b_i,a_j')=\sum_k q_{jk}(b_i,b_k')=q_{ji}.$$
Hence $Q=P^{T}$: **the change of basis matrix from $B'$ to $A'$ is the transpose of the change of basis matrix from $A$ to $B$.** Equivalently, the matrix from $A'$ to $B'$ is $(P^{T})^{-1}$, the inverse transpose. ∎

prompt:
Let $R$ be a not necessarily commutative ring with $1$.

(a) If $V_1, V_2, \dots, V_n$ are $n$ nonisomorphic irreducible right $R$-modules, show that there exists an $R$-module epimorphism from $R$, viewed as a right $R$-module, to the external direct sum $V_1 \oplus V_2 \oplus \cdots \oplus V_n$.

(b) Suppose $R$, viewed as a right $R$-module, has a finite composition series with nonisomorphic composition factors. Prove that the Jacobson radical of $R$ is equal to $0$.
answer: (a) Pick $0\ne v_i\in V_i$ and map $r\mapsto(v_1r,\dots,v_nr)$; a submodule of $\bigoplus V_i$ projecting onto every $V_i$ is everything (induction plus Schur's lemma). (b) Every simple module is a composition factor of $R_R$, so (a) gives an epimorphism $R\to\bigoplus V_i$ between modules of the same length $n$, hence an isomorphism; $J(R)$ annihilates every simple module, so $J(R)=1\cdot J(R)=0$.

solutions.title: A subdirect product of distinct simples is the full sum
solutions.body:
**Lemma.** Let $V_1,\dots,V_n$ be pairwise nonisomorphic simple right $R$-modules and let $M\subseteq V_1\oplus\cdots\oplus V_n$ be a submodule with $\pi_i(M)=V_i$ for every coordinate projection $\pi_i$. Then $M=V_1\oplus\cdots\oplus V_n$.

*Proof.* Induction on $n$; $n=1$ is clear. For $n>1$ let $\rho\colon M\to V_1\oplus\cdots\oplus V_{n-1}$ be the projection; $\rho(M)$ projects onto each $V_i$ ($i<n$), so by induction $\rho(M)=V_1\oplus\cdots\oplus V_{n-1}$. Now $\ker\rho=M\cap V_n$ is a submodule of the simple module $V_n$.
- If $M\cap V_n=V_n$, then $M\supseteq V_n$ and $M=M+V_n=\rho(M)\oplus V_n$ is everything.
- If $M\cap V_n=0$, then $\rho$ is an isomorphism and $\theta=\pi_n\circ\rho^{-1}\colon V_1\oplus\cdots\oplus V_{n-1}\to V_n$ is surjective. But for $i<n$ the restriction $\theta|_{V_i}\colon V_i\to V_n$ is $0$ or an isomorphism (Schur), and $V_i\not\cong V_n$, so it is $0$. Hence $\theta=0$, contradicting surjectivity onto $V_n\ne0$. $\square$

**(a)** Choose $0\ne v_i\in V_i$ and define $\phi\colon R\to V_1\oplus\cdots\oplus V_n$ by $\phi(r)=(v_1r,\dots,v_nr)$, a right $R$-module homomorphism. Since $V_i$ is simple, $v_iR=V_i$, so the image $M=\phi(R)$ satisfies $\pi_i(M)=V_i$ for all $i$. By the lemma, $\phi$ is onto.

**(b)** Let $0=I_0\subset I_1\subset\cdots\subset I_n=R$ be a composition series with pairwise nonisomorphic factors $V_i=I_i/I_{i-1}$.

*Every simple right module is isomorphic to some $V_i$.* A simple $V$ is $\cong R/M$ with $M=\mathrm{ann}(v)$ a maximal right ideal ($0\ne v\in V$). As a submodule of a module of finite length, $M$ has a composition series; appending $R$ gives a composition series of $R_R$ with $R/M$ as a factor. By Jordan–Hölder, $R/M\cong V_i$ for some $i$.

By (a) there is an epimorphism $\phi\colon R\to V_1\oplus\cdots\oplus V_n$. Both modules have composition length $n$, so $\ker\phi$ has length $0$, i.e. $\phi$ is an isomorphism.

The Jacobson radical $J=J(R)$ is the intersection of the maximal right ideals; for a simple module $V$ and $v\in V$, $\mathrm{ann}(v)$ is $R$ or a maximal right ideal, so $vJ=0$. Thus $J$ annihilates each $V_i$, hence annihilates $V_1\oplus\cdots\oplus V_n\cong R_R$. In particular $1\cdot J=0$, so $J=0$. ∎
